title: Harmonized Afrobarometer Variables: Cross-Round Mapping and Comparability Codes, Rounds 1–9
text:
The release
Afrobarometer’s round files name and code the same question differently across rounds. The mapping assigns the 1,897 round variables that recur in at least two of Rounds 1 to 9 to 386 common variables, with each round’s question text. The release also codes the comparability of the consumption model’s predictors by round and holds the code that rebuilds the harmonized file. The code runs on the round files that users download from Afrobarometer.

title: Harmonized Afrobarometer Variables: Cross-Round Mapping and Comparability Codes, Rounds 1–9
text:
The mapping
The original round files contain 2,954 variables. The 1,897 that recur in at least two rounds are mapped onto 386 common variables. A language model proposed cross-round matches from the question and label texts, and I checked every proposed match in each round against the variable name, the codebook entry and the question wording. The 1,887 written rules of the code reproduce the checked mapping. Appendix B of Estimating Economic Class in Afrobarometer Using Survey-to-Survey Imputation documents the rules and their verification.
The wording or the scope of a question can change while its common name stays. The comparability codes follow the scheme of Fortier et al. (2017) and compare Afrobarometer’s rounds with each other for the predictors of the consumption model.

The release
The release holds the predicted middle-class shares of 159,698 populated cells of 96 km² in 55 African countries, under six income definitions, with their sums for countries, provinces and districts. Incomes are per capita and per day, in constant 2016 US dollars at the purchasing power parities of the 2017 International Comparison Program, as the Gallup World Poll reports them. Every band includes its lower bound and excludes its upper bound. Banerjee and Duflo (2008) and Ravallion (2010) classify households by consumption, while the Gallup World Poll records income. The classes are therefore an income-based approximation to their concepts.

title: Mapping Africa’s Middle Class Across Space: cell-level data
text:
Method
For each of 829 subnational regions in 45 countries with at least 30 respondents, we compute the survey-weighted share of respondents in each band. We relate these shares to 102 features of the regions: points of interest and networks from the Africa Infrastructure Database (Krantz, 2023), population and its age structure, night lights, travel times, gridded GDP per capita and the Human Development Index (Kummu et al., 2018), and two wealth indices (Lee and Braithwaite, 2022; Chi et al., 2022). A Super Learner combines five learners (gradient boosting, XGBoost, random forests, neural networks and a generalized linear model), with folds that leave out one country at a time. We then evaluate the fitted model at the features of each cell.
Within each district, or province where the data have no districts, one shift on the logit scale makes the population-weighted average of the cell predictions equal the ensemble’s prediction for that district. Population comes from WorldPop (Pezzulo et al., 2017), and from GHS-POP (Schiavina et al., 2023) where WorldPop records none (1,084 cells). The share times the population of a cell gives its number of middle-class people.

title: Mapping Africa’s Middle Class Across Space: cell-level data
text:
Accuracy
In cross-validation that leaves out one country at a time, the R² is 0.72 for the Banerjee and Duflo (2008) band and 0.62 for the Kharas (2010) band, and it lies between 0.49 and 0.72 across the six definitions. This measures accuracy in a country without survey data. For 172 test regions withheld from estimation, the R² lies between 0.65 and 0.88 on the logit scale on which the models are fit. These regions measure accuracy for new regions of surveyed countries. Both compare predictions with regional averages. Within countries, the model explains 46 percent of the variation in regional shares for the $2–10 band and 3 percent for the $10–100 band.

title: Mapping Africa’s Middle Class Across Space: cell-level data
text:
Reading the cells
The cell values are predictions. Every survey share behind them is a regional average, and the models learn how features and middle-class shares move together across regions. The cell maps assume that the same relation holds within regions. The sums for districts, provinces and countries are the firmest numbers in the release, and the district shares equal the ensemble’s predictions for the districts by construction.
Three groups of cells carry a flag. In ten countries (Angola, Cabo Verde, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe, Seychelles, Sudan and Western Sahara), the cells rest on the relation estimated in other countries (surveyed_country is false). For 2,066 cells on coasts and lake shores whose center lies outside every administrative polygon, we use the nearest region of the same country (nearest_unit is true). For 1,084 cells, the population comes from GHS-POP (population_gapfilled is true). The columns model_sd_* give the standard deviation of the five learners’ predictions for a cell and rank cells by how much the learners disagree.

Population is from WorldPop and GHS-POP, both under CC BY 4.0. The hexagons are the grid of the Africa Infrastructure Database (Krantz, 2023). Administrative codes and names follow GADM 4.1. title: Estimating Economic Class in Afrobarometer Using Survey-to-Survey Imputation
text:
Abstract


Afrobarometer, the principal pan-African attitude survey, omits consumption and income. As a result, the economic class of its respondents is unknown. I impute consumption into Afrobarometer using a model estimated on 49 household-expenditure surveys in 25 countries, with 100 draws per respondent calibrated to the World Bank’s national distributions. Each draw is classified under five published middle-class definitions, for adults in Rounds 8 and 9 (the adult series) and for households in Rounds 3 to 9 (the household series). In hold-out tests, the share at or above the Banerjee–Duflo upper bracket has a mean absolute error of 2.3 percentage points for an excluded survey wave and 7.0 for an excluded country. That share averages 28.5 percent across adult country-rounds, and bounded middle-class shares run from 9.8 to 68.5 percent across definitions. In the household series the middle-class share is higher by a median of 25.2 points in urban than in rural households and by 23.7 points for respondents with secondary education.

title: Where the Windfall Lands: Export Booms and the Demand for Democracy in Africa
text:
Job market paper Last updated November 2026
Paper

title: Where the Windfall Lands: Export Booms and the Demand for Democracy in Africa
text:
Abstract


Do economic windfalls strengthen popular demand for democracy? Modernization theory predicts that higher household incomes increase demand for democracy by reducing reliance on political patrons, while rentier theories predict that windfalls captured by the state reinforce patronage and dependence. I link 125,659 Afrobarometer respondents (2005–2022) in 2,198 districts of 22 African countries to baseline crop maps and world prices. In a shift-share design that controls for expected price exposure, I compare districts with higher and lower shares of residents employed in farming. I find that demand for democracy rises more in districts where more residents farm when world prices of their export crops rise. For a one-standard-deviation three-year boom, the response is 0.025 standard deviations higher in a district with a 25-percentage-point higher farming share (p = 0.061 under a randomization test over the six price series). This is consistent with windfalls supporting democracy where they reach households and equally with state patronage lowering demand where few residents farm.

title: Sékou Metiki
text:
About
I am a researcher at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy and a doctoral candidate in Quantitative Economics at Kiel University, where I submitted my dissertation in November 2026. My research is in development economics and political economy, and most of it is on African countries.
Most African countries lack the tax and administrative-register data used to record incomes in high-income countries, and household surveys that measure consumption are expensive and infrequent. Much of my work therefore starts with measurement. With Tobias Heidland, I map where Africa’s middle class lives: a machine-learning model predicts middle-class shares for almost 160,000 populated cells from survey incomes, infrastructure, night lights and population data. In a second paper, I impute household consumption into Afrobarometer, the principal pan-African attitude survey. The data of both papers are public on Zenodo.
I use these measures to study how economic gains relate to political attitudes. My job market paper asks whether citizens’ demand for democracy changes when export gains are more likely to reach households. A separate paper with Tobias Heidland and Lukas Menkhoff measures how central banks prepare for foreign exchange intervention and has been revised and resubmitted to the Journal of Money, Credit and Banking.

title: Research
text: My research asks who benefits from export booms in African economies: how much of a rise in world crop prices reaches farming households, how much the state retains, and how citizens’ demand for democracy responds. I also develop methods to measure household living standards where expenditure and administrative data are limited.

title: Research
text:
Under Review


Preparing for FX Intervention
with Tobias Heidland and Lukas Menkhoff
Revised and resubmitted, Journal of Money, Credit and Banking Last updated November 2026

Between 2001 and 2020, preparedness rose with more rigid regimes and larger reserves, while aggregate intervention did not keep pace.

Paper

Most central banks do not publish their foreign exchange interventions (FXI), but the preparations that enable their interventions are visible. We measure FXI preparedness through three policy decisions, namely the rigidity of the exchange rate regime, the level of official reserves relative to GDP and the share of reserves held in assets available for intervention. For the last of these, we build a new index from the IMF’s data on reserve composition. Better-prepared countries intervene more, so preparedness indicates a willingness to intervene where intervention data are not published. Between 2001 and 2020, preparedness rose with more rigid regimes and larger reserves, while aggregate intervention did not keep pace. Preparedness is higher in economies with lower income, greater trade openness and more volatile portfolio inflows.

Mapping Africa’s Middle Class Across Space
with Tobias Heidland
Working paper Last updated November 2026

In leave-one-country-out cross-validation, the model explains 72 percent of the regional variation in the share of people living on $2–10 a day and 62 percent for $10–100 a day.

Paper · Data

We provide the first highly granular mapping of the African middle class. title: Economic Class of Afrobarometer Respondents: Imputed Consumption under Five Middle-Class Definitions, Rounds 3–9
text:
The release
Afrobarometer, the principal pan-African survey of public attitudes, records no consumption or income. The economic class of its respondents is therefore unknown. I impute consumption per person per day, in 2021 PPP dollars, into Afrobarometer respondents from a model estimated on 49 household-expenditure surveys from 25 countries. Each respondent receives 100 draws calibrated to the national distributions of the World Bank’s Poverty and Inequality Platform. Five published middle-class definitions then classify every draw on the same consumption scale: Banerjee and Duflo, Ravallion, López-Calva and Ortiz-Juárez, the African Development Bank, and Birdsall. The method is described in Estimating Economic Class in Afrobarometer Using Survey-to-Survey Imputation.
The household series covers 302,595 respondents in 42 countries and 215 country-rounds of Rounds 3 to 9. The adult series covers 100,113 respondents in 39 countries and 73 country-rounds of Rounds 8 and 9, for adult citizens. In hold-out tests, the share at or above the Banerjee–Duflo upper bracket has a mean absolute error of 2.3 percentage points for an excluded survey wave and 7.0 for an excluded country.

The respondent-level draws, the continuous consumption panel and the sub-national estimates link to Afrobarometer respondents or derive from Afrobarometer’s restricted geocodes. I share them on request under Afrobarometer’s terms, after the requester has written to me with the intended use.

title: Economic Class of Afrobarometer Respondents: Imputed Consumption under Five Middle-Class Definitions, Rounds 3–9
text:
Method
The model predicts consumption from items that Afrobarometer shares with the base surveys: durable assets, education, urban residence and dwelling characteristics, with satellite measures at the respondent’s location or administrative area and national GDP. The draws carry the uncertainty of the model’s coefficients, of its country and area effects and of the residual. Part of the residual is shared within an enumeration area. Each draw is then calibrated to the Poverty and Inequality Platform’s national distribution for the country-round. The published thresholds are 2005 PPP dollars, converted to 2021 PPP with the ratio of US consumer prices, 1.3875.
Standard errors combine sampling variance, imputation variance, the line-up’s level error and, where estimated, the model term. The files report each component separately. The shares in the release are already pooled over the draws. A statistic computed from the respondent draws is estimated in each draw and pooled by Rubin’s rules. A regression of an outcome on imputed class estimates an association with the model’s prediction.

title: Economic Class of Afrobarometer Respondents: Imputed Consumption under Five Middle-Class Definitions, Rounds 3–9
text:
Sources
The release uses Afrobarometer data from Rounds 3 to 9, AidData’s geocoding of Afrobarometer (BenYishay et al., 2017), household-expenditure surveys obtained under their producers’ terms, and the World Bank’s Poverty and Inequality Platform.

title: Economic Class of Afrobarometer Respondents: Imputed Consumption under Five Middle-Class Definitions, Rounds 3–9
text:
Related data

Harmonized Afrobarometer Variables: the cross-round mapping of Afrobarometer’s variables on which the release builds, with the code that rebuilds the harmonized file.
Mapping Africa’s Middle Class Across Space: cell-level data: middle-class shares from Gallup World Poll incomes. Consumption here and income there are different measures of welfare, and each set of shares is meant to be used on its own.
